method_in_plain_language: 1. Before looking at any result, a rule was written down and frozen for choosing 60 papers about medical-device technology that involve five named firms. The rule pins the query, the date window (2020-01-01 to 2022-12-31), the sort order, the tie-break, and a fixed fallback ladder, so the sample cannot be adjusted after the fact. It produced 60 works with 60 distinct DOIs, twelve per firm.

2. Each of those 60 DOIs was then looked up, one work at a time, in OpenAlex, Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed and OpenAIRE, and in one batch call to Semantic Scholar. Whatever each source returned was saved verbatim.

3. A 'source row' is one record a database returned for one anchor. A 'distinct work' is a unique DOI (falling back to PMID, then to the OpenAlex work id) across all of those rows. The ratio of the second to the first is how much genuinely different information the multi-database fetch bought.
4. Identifiers were only recorded when they literally appeared in a saved response. Nothing was derived, resolved or inferred from another scheme.
5. Titles, author counts and publication dates were then compared across databases for the same DOI and left unrepaired. Every difference is a measurement.

what_this_measures: 308 records came back from six databases, but they describe only 60 distinct works: a de-duplication ratio of 0.195, meaning a naive union would over-count by roughly 5.1x. The 60 anchors are spread across the databases very unevenly: openalex holds 60/60, crossref holds 59/60, europepmc holds 37/60, pubmed_eutils holds 37/60, semantic_scholar holds 56/60, openaire holds 59/60. Only 1 different source-counts appear at all, and 36 anchors are held by all six sources.
what_this_cannot_support: It cannot say which database is 'complete'. The sample was drawn FROM OpenAlex, so OpenAlex trivially holds 60/60. The 37/60 and 56/60 figures are coverage of an OpenAlex-defined sample, not of the literature.
It cannot rank databases by quality. A missing record may be a scope decision (Europe PMC indexes biomedical work only), not a defect.
It cannot claim research value from row counts. The only research-relevant quantity here is the disagreement structure, not the volume.
notable_observations: Cross-identifier links are clean: for 38 of 60 anchors a single PMID is agreed by every source that exposes one, and 0 anchors have two different PMIDs for the same DOI. 22 anchors have no PMID in any source.

Titles are less stable than identifiers: 24 anchors have byte-identical titles after whitespace/case normalisation, 27 have titles where one is a prefix of another (a truncation signature), and 9 have titles that differ in substance, all for the same DOI.

OpenAIRE's de-duplicated research products can carry SEVERAL DOIs (9 of 59 records here, e.g. a Spanish and an English version of the same article). A reader that takes 'the first DOI' in such a record mis-assigns the work; this connector records the queried DOI as primary and lists the rest.

Semantic Scholar's batch endpoint ignores the field projection unless `fields` is passed as a QUERY parameter, and silently returns only {paperId,title} with HTTP 200 otherwise. That is a silent partial response, not an error, and it is recorded in the probe evidence.
